title: Planning the application
goals: Turn requirements into checkable acceptance cases
Plan a feasible pipeline and human review

prerequisite.prompt: Why must a recommendation show no eligible option when every item fails a hard constraint?
prerequisite.answer: Otherwise it would silently violate the stated requirement.

vocabulary: A statement of behavior the application must provide
An input and expected behavior used to judge a requirement
A limited implementation for testing a design

blocks.text: Plan a fictional activity chooser for a teacher-supervised 20-minute session. It will validate a small local dataset, exclude over-limit items, rank eligible items using 2 * fun + learning and break ties alphabetically. It will explain the result for human review. It will not book, message or collect personal student profiles.

blocks.title: Follow the evidence
rows: Filter then score then tie rule
blocks.caption: Read each row from left to right and connect the evidence to the stated rule.

blocks.text: Define fields name, minutes, fun and learning. Require a nonempty text name, integer minutes 0 through 60 and integer ratings 0 through 5. Reject duplicate names because the tie rule uses names as identifiers. Write cases before implementing so requirements do not drift to fit outputs.

blocks.label: Write an acceptance case for the duration boundary and one for no eligible option.

blocks.text: A requirement such as make a smart choice cannot be tested precisely. Replace it with a stated score, limit, tie rule and output explanation. If real feedback later changes the policy, record a versioned change rather than rewriting previous evidence.

The scope is a rule-based prototype using fictional ratings. It does not demonstrate personalized learning impact or a trained AI model. A clear non-goal protects students from building an untestable or overly broad project.

blocks.label: Name two capabilities excluded from this prototype and explain why.

workbook.title: Name the user need
workbook.prompt: State the purpose and decision owner of the worked chooser.
workbook.answer: Suggest a suitable eligible activity for a teacher-supervised session; the teacher reviews and decides.

workbook.title: Write an acceptance case
workbook.prompt: Give a tie case for A and B with score 8 each and valid durations.
workbook.answer: With both eligible, choose A alphabetically regardless of input order.

workbook.title: Repair vague scope
workbook.prompt: Replace the requirement always choose the best activity with a checkable one.
workbook.answer: Choose the highest 2 * fun + learning score among valid items within the limit, using alphabetical ties; return no eligible option if none qualify.

workbook.title: Plan independently
workbook.prompt: Plan a 15-minute fictional club chooser. Specify schema, score, duration limit, tie rule, invalid-data behavior, output and three acceptance cases.
workbook.answer: Retain the stated schema and scoring or justify an explicit alternative. Require boundary 15/16, tie/order and no-match cases with expected results, rejection reasons and human review.

workbook.title: State non-goals
workbook.prompt: Name two capabilities excluded from this prototype and explain why.
workbook.answer: Examples: real student profiling, automatic booking or claims of proven learning benefit. They need separate evidence, permissions and scope.

teacher.background: Teach Week 31 as a two-session investigation using fictional data. Plan a fictional activity chooser for a teacher-supervised 20-minute session. It will validate a small local dataset, exclude over-limit items, rank eligible items using 2 * fun + learning and break ties alphabetically. It will explain the result for human review. It will not book, message or collect personal student profiles. Assess the three stated outcomes through the independent task, not by copying the worked result.
materials: Python 3 editor with a fresh local practice file
Paper trace table and the student workbook
Fictional input records from this lesson; no real student identifiers
sessions: Retrieve the prerequisite and explain the purpose in the opening section.
Read the worked example and diagram; ask learners to trace each step aloud.
Complete W1 and W2, then compare predictions with observed results.
Collect the guided prediction before running; discuss a mismatch and its cause.
Retrieve the main rule without showing the previous answer.
Use W3 to diagnose and repair the stated failure; rerun an earlier case.
Collect W4 independently, including code or plan, predictions and explanations, before hints.
Discuss W5 and the exit; use the fresh retry when support was needed.
teacher.guidedAnswer: An otherwise valid 20-minute item qualifies; a 21-minute-only dataset yields no eligible option under limit 20. Exit: Examples: real student profiling, automatic booking or claims of proven learning benefit. They need separate evidence, permissions and scope.
